summary: Discusses diversity and professional conduct in the IETF. It notes that early participation was largely a small, homogeneous group and argues for broader participation and respectful conduct.

eli5.summary: This note says everyone should feel welcome in the group and that people should behave respectfully.

questions: what is the ietf stance on diversity
what is professional conduct in the ietf
how do you handle harassment in the ietf
why does diversity matter in standards development
subtitle: Building a more welcoming and respectful standards community

tldr.problem: The IETF has historically been dominated by a narrow demographic of well-funded American male technicians, and aggressive or hostile interaction styles have been tolerated, which deters diverse participation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC advocates for intentional efforts to ensure both participant diversity (varied backgrounds in the group) and participation diversity (constructive engagement from all members), along with clear policies against harassment and bullying.
tldr.outcome: Greater diversity in participation improves decision-making and innovation, so the IETF must move from cultural tolerance of aggressive behavior to creating a safe, professional environment for an increasingly diverse community.

today: RFC 7704 is an Informational document that remains a key reference for discussions about IETF culture. The IESG's anti-harassment policy and the diversity initiatives it prompted continue to guide the organization's efforts to be more welcoming to people from all backgrounds and to enforce standards of professional conduct.

sections.title: The IETF's History and Current Culture
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force evolved from a small, government-funded research community in the 1960s and 1980s to an open standards body in the late 1980s. From the start, participation was predominantly white, male, and American. The RFC argues that the aggressive and sometimes hostile debate style that developed in this homogeneous environment persists, even as the IETF's membership has become more diverse.

The document notes that aggressive discussion is common within the IETF, and people who complain about hostile behavior are often criticized for being too sensitive, rather than the aggressive party being asked to change. This culture has been sustained by a management structure that exhibits selection bias, favoring those who are already well-known and comfortable with the existing style.
sections.eli5: The IETF started as a small, tight-knit group of people who are very similar to each other. Over time, more different kinds of people joined, but the group did not change how it talks to each other. People still argue very aggressively, which makes new people feel unwelcome.

sections.title: Why Diversity and Respectful Conduct Matter
sections.content:
The RFC establishes that diversity has two dimensions: participant diversity (the variety of people in the group) and participation diversity (the variety and quality of ideas discussed). Research cited in the document shows that groups with greater diversity make better decisions and perform better at complex tasks because they bring different bases of knowledge and challenge each other's assumptions.

The aggressive style of interaction, while it may reflect long-standing tradition, is harmful. Many people from polite cultures find aggressive debate alienating and withdraw from participation. The document also notes that both overt harassment (based on protected characteristics like gender or race) and targeted bullying (focused attacks on individuals) reduce diversity by discouraging participation.
sections.eli5: Different people have different ideas, and when everyone thinks differently, the group comes up with better solutions. But when people are mean or aggressive, others stop trying to help, which makes everything worse.

sections.title: Harassment, Bullying, and Inclusive Participation
sections.content:
The RFC defines harassment as biased treatment based on demographic characteristics (race, gender, religion, sexual orientation), while bullying is targeted intimidation of specific individuals. Both tactics can range from subtle (ignoring someone) to overt (aggressive attacks). The document describes how bullying in workplaces is characterized by belittling, excessive monitoring, undermining, exclusion, and targeted hostility.

To support constructive participation, the IETF must ensure access to materials and discussions, engage diverse participants seriously, facilitate the contribution of timid speakers, and actively shut down derogatory communication styles. This requires balance: the IETF must not sacrifice work efficiency, but it must recognize that inclusive practices often uncover issues that skilled participants miss.
sections.eli5: There are different ways people are mean: some are mean because of what someone looks like, and some are mean to one person in particular. The IETF needs rules that say no one gets to be mean, and people should help new people feel comfortable joining in.

sections.title: Addressing Unconstructive Participation
sections.content:
When problematic participants cannot be ignored because their behavior is too disruptive or offensive, the RFC argues that personal intervention rarely works and management action is required. The IETF has formal policies: an anti-harassment policy enforced by an Ombudsperson, mailing list moderation guidelines, and working group chair authority. The challenge is that these policies have meaning only if enforced consistently.

The document emphasizes that abusive behavior can be stopped if the community and management work together to enforce consequences. Without enforcement, policies signal ideals but fail to change behavior. The IETF community must collaborate to communicate clearly that harassment and bullying will not be tolerated.
sections.eli5: The IETF has rules that say people should not be mean, and there is someone called an Ombudsperson who helps when people break the rules. But the rules only work if people actually use them to stop the mean behavior.

sections.title: The Security Argument for Diversity and Conduct
sections.content:
The RFC argues that the security of the IETF's credibility depends on its role as an open, productive venue for collaborative technical development. More diverse scrutiny of standards improves technical rigor and quality. Additionally, the legal liability of operating an organization with a hostile environment creates further incentive to adopt and enforce behavioral policies.

The quality of technical documents ultimately depends on the security of the process that creates them. A process that welcomes diverse participation and treats participants with respect produces better outcomes and maintains the IETF's distinctive reputation as a standards organization that works.
sections.eli5: If the IETF keeps being mean to people, eventually no one will trust the standards it makes. So being nice and welcoming helps keep the IETF strong and important.

references.text: Kellogg Insight, "Better Decisions Through Diversity: Heterogeneity can boost group performance", Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, October 2010.
